pool.q: What is descriptive statistics?
options: Drawing conclusions about a population from a sample
Predicting future values with a model
pool.explain: Inferential statistics then uses samples to draw conclusions about populations.
pool.evidence: Organizing, summarizing, and presenting data is called descriptive statistics

pool.q: Data that are the result of counting are called…
pool.explain: Counts are discrete; measurements that can take any value on an interval are continuous.
pool.evidence: All data that are the result of counting are called quantitative discrete data.

pool.q: When studying the effect one variable may have on another, what is the first variable called?
pool.explain: The explanatory variable may explain changes in the response variable.
pool.evidence: we call the first variable the explanatory variable and the second the response variable

pool.q: Why are treatments assigned to subjects at random in an experiment?
options: To spread potential lurking variables equally among the groups
To avoid needing a control group
pool.explain: Randomisation is what lets experiments suggest cause and effect.
pool.evidence: When subjects are assigned treatments randomly, all of the potential lurking variables are spread equally among the groups.

pool.q: How should a researcher design an experiment comparing groups?
options: So each group gets several treatments
So the groups differ in as many ways as possible
So only volunteers who expect results take part
So the only difference between the groups is the planned treatment
pool.explain: Any other difference could explain the outcome instead.
pool.evidence: The researcher must design their experiment in such a way that there is only one difference between groups being compared: the planned treatments.

pool.q: What should a sample have in common with its population?
options: The same characteristics as the population it represents
pool.explain: A representative sample lets us generalise to the population.
pool.evidence: we typically use a sample of the population which should have the same characteristics as the population it is representing

pool.q: Why is systematic sampling often chosen?
options: It needs no list of the population
pool.explain: It picks every kth member from an ordered list.
pool.evidence: Systematic sampling is frequently chosen because it is a simple method.

pool.q: With a large population, how does sampling without replacement compare with sampling with replacement?
pool.explain: The chance of picking someone twice is very low.
pool.evidence: sampling without replacement is approximately the same as sampling with replacement because the chance of picking the same individual more than once with replacement is very low

pool.q: Why can a graph be more effective than a mass of numbers?
options: Graphs replace the need for data
You can see where data cluster and where there are few values
pool.explain: Graphs reveal the distribution's shape at a glance.
pool.evidence: A graph can be a more effective way of presenting data than a mass of numbers because we can see where data clusters and where there are only a few data values.

pool.q: Which two graphs are used to display categorical data?
pool.explain: Categories are shown as wedges (pie) or bars proportional to their counts or percentages.
pool.evidence: Two graphs that are used to display categorical data are pie charts and bar graphs.

pool.q: What can an outlier indicate?
options: That the mean is always zero
A recording mistake, or that something unusual is happening
That the sample is too large
pool.explain: Writing 50 instead of 500 is an example of a mistake.
pool.evidence: Some outliers are due to mistakes (for example, writing down 50 instead of 500) while others may indicate that something unusual is happening.

pool.q: What is often the first step when examining quantitative data?
options: Putting it in a frequency table
pool.explain: Frequency tables lead naturally to histograms.
pool.evidence: The first thing we may do, especially for quantitative data, is to examine it in a frequency table.

pool.q: Why is the median often a better measure of centre than the mean when there are outliers?
options: It is always larger than the mean
It is more robust — not affected by the exact values of the outliers
It is easier to calculate by hand
pool.explain: One extreme value can pull the mean a long way but barely moves the median.
pool.evidence: The median is generally a better measure of the center when there are extreme values or outliers because it is more robust

pool.q: When is the standard deviation small?
options: When the data are all concentrated close to the mean
When the data are skewed to the right
pool.explain: Standard deviation measures how far values typically fall from the mean.
pool.evidence: The standard deviation is small when the data are all concentrated close to the mean, exhibiting little variation or spread.

pool.q: You score at the 90th percentile. What does that mean?
options: 90% of scores are the same as or lower than yours
10% of scores are lower than yours
pool.explain: Percentiles describe position, not percentage correct.
pool.evidence: It means that 90% of test scores are the same or less than your score and 10% of the test scores are the same or greater than your test score.

pool.q: When might a low percentile be a good result?
options: On a timed exam, where finishing quickly is better
pool.explain: Whether high or low is good depends on what is measured.
pool.evidence: A low percentile could be considered good, as finishing more quickly on a timed exam is desirable.

pool.q: What do measures of location quantify?
options: How spread out the data are
Where an observation stands relative to the rest of the distribution
pool.explain: Percentiles and quartiles are measures of location.
pool.evidence: Measures of location are a tool used to quantify where an observation stands in relation to the rest of the distribution.

pool.q: What range of values can a probability take?
pool.explain: 0 means impossible; 1 means certain.
pool.evidence: Probabilities are between zero and one, inclusive

pool.q: When is an experiment a probability experiment?
options: When the result is not predetermined
When it happens in a laboratory
pool.explain: Rolling a die is a classic example.
pool.evidence: If the result is not predetermined, then the experiment is said to be a probability experiment

pool.q: What is probability?
options: A measure of how certain we are about the outcomes of an experiment
pool.explain: It quantifies uncertainty.
pool.evidence: Probability is a measure that is associated with how certain we are of outcomes of a particular experiment or activity.

pool.q: Klaus can afford only one holiday: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.35. What is P(A OR B)?
pool.explain: For mutually exclusive events you can simply add the probabilities.

pool.q: Why is P(A AND B) = 0 in Klaus's holiday example?
options: He can only take one holiday, so the events are mutually exclusive
pool.explain: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together.
pool.evidence: because Klaus can only afford to take one vacation

pool.q: What should you assume about two events at the start of a problem?
options: That they are neither mutually exclusive nor independent
That they are always mutually exclusive
pool.explain: Only change the assumption when the information supports it.
pool.evidence: We must always go into a problem assuming two events are not mutually exclusive or independent

pool.q: In a binomial experiment, how many outcomes are possible on each trial?
options: Exactly two, called success and failure
As many as the number of trials
pool.explain: A binomial setting also needs a fixed number of independent trials with the same probability of success.
pool.evidence: There are only two possible outcomes, called “success” and “failure,” for each trial.

pool.q: In a normal distribution, how do the mean and median compare?
options: They are the same, because the curve is symmetric
pool.explain: Symmetry puts both at the centre.
pool.evidence: In theory, the mean is the same as the median, because the graph is symmetric about

pool.q: How many normal distributions are there?
pool.explain: Each combination of mean and standard deviation gives a different one.
pool.evidence: This means there are an infinite number of normal probability distributions.

pool.q: Which distribution does the text call the most important of all?
pool.explain: Many natural measurements and sample means follow it.
pool.evidence: The normal or "Gaussian" distribution is the most important of all the distributions

pool.q: What are the main forms of statistical inference?
options: Point estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing
pool.explain: Inference generalises from a sample to a population.
pool.evidence: The main forms of Inference are: Point estimation confidence interval Hypothesis testing

pool.q: As the sample size grows, what happens to the spread of the sample means?
pool.explain: This is the Central Limit Theorem at work: averages of larger samples vary less.
pool.evidence: The spread of the sample means (the standard deviation of the sample means) gets smaller.

pool.q: What is a confidence interval?
options: The single best guess for a parameter
An estimate that is an interval of numbers rather than just one number
The probability that the hypothesis is true
The range of the sample data
pool.explain: The interval is random; the population parameter it tries to capture is fixed.
pool.evidence: A confidence interval is another type of estimate but, instead of being just one number, it is an interval of numbers.

pool.q: With confidence intervals, which part is random and which is fixed?
options: The parameter is random; the interval is fixed
The interval is random; the population parameter is fixed
pool.explain: Different samples give different intervals around the same true value.
pool.evidence: the confidence interval itself is a random variable, while the population parameter is fixed

pool.q: What is the alternative hypothesis (Ha)?
options: The same as the null hypothesis
A claim that contradicts H0, which we conclude when we reject H0
A guess made after the data are collected
pool.explain: The null hypothesis is the starting assumption.
pool.evidence: It is a claim about the population that is contradictory to H 0 and what we conclude when we reject H 0

pool.q: Since the null and alternative hypotheses contradict each other, what must you do?
options: Examine the evidence to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis
pool.explain: The data decide, not personal preference.
pool.evidence: you must examine evidence to decide if you have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis or not

pool.q: What is a Type I error?
options: Not rejecting H0 when H0 is false
Rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true
Taking a sample that is too small
pool.explain: A Type II error is the opposite: failing to reject a false H0.
pool.evidence: The decision is to reject H 0 when H 0 is true (incorrect decision known as a Type I error ).

pool.q: Which kind of question can linear regression and correlation help answer?
options: Whether a mechanic's salary is related to their work experience
How many people live in a city
Which day of the week it is
pool.explain: They describe relationships between two quantitative variables.
pool.evidence: Linear regression and correlation can help you determine if an auto mechanic’s salary is related to his work experience.

pool.q: What values can the correlation coefficient r take?
pool.explain: Values near −1 or +1 indicate a strong linear relationship.
pool.evidence: The value of r is always between –1 and +1

pool.q: What does the correlation coefficient r measure?
options: How strong a linear relationship between x and y is
pool.explain: Correlation does not prove causation.
pool.evidence: then r can measure how strong the linear relationship is

pool.q: What is the process of fitting the best-fit line called?
pool.explain: Regression finds the line that best predicts y from x.
pool.evidence: This process of fitting the best-fit line is called linear regression

pool.q: Why shouldn't you use a regression line to predict y for an x value far outside the sample's range?
options: Because regression lines only work for negative slopes
Because the correlation would become exactly 1
Because the line has no y-intercept there
Because that x value is outside the domain of the x-values in the sample data
pool.explain: Predicting beyond the observed range (extrapolation) assumes the pattern continues, which may not be true.
pool.evidence: because 50 is not within the domain of the x -values in the sample data

pool.q: What is interpolation?
options: Predicting far outside the observed range
Predicting within the range of the observed x values
pool.explain: Predicting outside the range is extrapolation, which is risky.
pool.evidence: The process of predicting inside of the observed x values observed in the data is called interpolation.

pool.q: What should you always do before fitting a regression line?
pool.explain: The plot shows whether a linear model makes sense.
pool.evidence: Remember, it is always important to plot a scatter diagram first.

pool.q: When is it reasonable to use linear regression methods?
options: When the scatterplot suggests a linear relationship
pool.explain: Curved patterns need different models.
pool.evidence: If the scatter plot indicates that there is a linear relationship between the variables, then it is reasonable to use the methods we are discussing.
